music_cards_altered_three_text: Each voicing puts tension tones on the G dominant of a ii-V-I in C. The tones are named against the chord: b9 is the 9th lowered a half step, #11 the 11th raised, and 13 the 6th an octave up. Tap Next for each voicing.
music_cards_altered_three_title: Three ways to colour the V
music_cards_altered_what_text: {first} is "{firstLabel}": {firstHint} {second} is "{secondLabel}": {secondHint} The third is an upper structure: a {triad} triad, a major triad a whole step above the root, over a 1 3 7 shell, adding the {adds}.
music_cards_bb_check_text: Check hides the notes. Find the box's root, then find the other notes by their roles around it.
music_cards_bb_six_text: This box is six notes around one root: the {roles}. The drill's root fret is the root note on string 6, and the box's own root is on string {string}, {place}{tuning}. Tap Hear it for the box low string to high.
music_cards_boxes_notes: with {perString} notes on each of the {count} strings
music_cards_boxes_one_text: A box of the minor pentatonic is one hand position{notes}. Here is box 1{tuning}, as the drill places it at its lowest root fret. The drill plays a box from the low string to the high.
music_cards_boxes_one_title: A box is a hand position
music_cards_boxes_up_text: The five boxes climb the neck. Counted from the root fret on string 6{tuning}, the lowest fret of {list}. In Check the notes stay hidden, so know where each box starts.
music_cards_cadence_pull_text: The 7th of V7 falls a half step to the 3rd of the tonic chord. The 3rd of V7 rises a half step to the tonic. That pull is what to listen for in Check, where the keys stay dark.
music_cards_cadence_raised_text: The V7 chord needs the 7th note raised by a half step: {raised} instead of {natural} in {tonic}. That raised note is the 3rd of V7 and leads up to the tonic. Tap each to hear it.
music_cards_cadence_roman_text: A Roman numeral names a chord by the scale degree its root sits on: I is the chord on the 1st note, IV on the 4th and V on the 5th. Capitals mean a major chord. Here are I IV I V7 I in {tonic}.
music_cards_cadence_roman_text_minor: A Roman numeral names a chord by the scale degree its root sits on: i is the chord on the 1st note, iv on the 4th and V on the 5th. Small letters mean a minor chord and capitals a major one. Here are i iv i V7 i in {tonic}.
music_cards_cadence_v7_note: Root, 3rd and 7th, with the 5th left out.
music_cards_caged_check_text: Check hides the notes of the shape. Know which shape it is, which strings it uses and where it sits. Then play it from its lowest string up.
music_cards_caged_five_text: CAGED names five shapes for a major chord, after the open chords C, A, G, E and D. Each one plays the same chord, in five places along the neck. Tap Next for where each sits{tuning}, counted from the root fret on string 6.
music_cards_caged_step: The {letter} shape uses strings {first} to {last}, and its lowest fret is {place}.
music_cards_charleston_count_text: Check hides what to play, so count it yourself: {counts}, and nothing else in the bar. Leaving the other beats empty is what lets the right hand's line stand out.
music_cards_charleston_hits_text: The Charleston is two left-hand hits in a bar: {hits}. Each hit is the left hand's two notes together, such as {a} and {b} over {chord}. Then the hand rests until the next bar.
music_cards_circle_analysis_iivi_text: A minor chord a fourth below a dominant is its ii, and the dominant resolves to the I.
music_cards_circle_analysis_key_text: For each chord you name the key it belongs to and its job there, such as ii, V or I. The example is Fly Me to the Moon. It starts in C.
music_cards_circle_analysis_subs_text: A dominant a half step above the I it resolves to is a tritone sub, like Db7 to C. A dominant a whole step below is a backdoor, like Bb7 to C.
music_cards_circle_analysis_v_of_text: A dominant that resolves to a chord other than the home key's I is a secondary dominant, a V of. A minor chord before it is a related ii.
music_cards_circle_borrowed_four_text: Tap each to hear the borrowed chord, then C. Each one takes a note from C minor.
music_cards_circle_borrowed_parallel_tex: A major key and the minor key on the same tonic are parallels, C major and C minor. The minor has three more flats. Borrowed chords come from it into the major key.
music_cards_circle_borrowed_spot_text: A borrowed chord holds a note outside the major scale. Look for a flat 3, flat 6 or flat 7 over the tonic.
music_cards_circle_chords_any_text: Pick any key and the wedge moves with it. The chords change, the numerals don't.
music_cards_circle_chords_pattern_text: The seven chords of a major key always run {numerals}. In C they are {names}. Tap Next to hear them.
music_cards_circle_chords_pattern_title: One pattern in every major key
music_cards_circle_chords_wedge_text: I, IV and V are the key and its two neighbours. The minor chords ii, iii and vi are the relative minors of IV, V and I.
music_cards_circle_count_flat_one: {key} major has 1 flat, {flat}. There's no second-to-last, so learn it.
music_cards_circle_count_flat_step: {accidentals}. The second-to-last is {flat}, so the key is {key}.
music_cards_circle_count_flat_text: A flat key takes its name from the second-to-last flat. The exception is F, with 1 flat, which you have to learn.
music_cards_circle_count_round_text: Start at C, which has no sharps or flats. Each step clockwise adds one sharp. Tap Next to walk round.
music_cards_circle_count_sharp_step: {accidentals}. The last is {last}, a half step up is {key}.
music_cards_circle_count_sharp_text: The major key is a half step above the last sharp. Find the last sharp in the signature, then go up one half step.
music_cards_circle_key_has_none: {key} major has no sharps or flats.
music_cards_circle_neighbours_ccw_text: One step counter-clockwise is a fourth up and adds one flat (or removes one sharp).
music_cards_circle_neighbours_cw_text: One step clockwise is a fifth up and adds one sharp (or removes one flat). Tap Next to see three steps.
music_cards_circle_neighbours_rel_step: {major} major has {minor} minor as its relative.
music_cards_circle_neighbours_rel_text: The relative minor sits on the middle ring, 3 half steps below the major tonic. The key across the wheel is a tritone away.
music_cards_circle_order_counting_text: A key with N sharps uses the first N in the order. A key with N flats uses the first N flats.
music_cards_circle_order_flats_text: Flats use the same letters in reverse: {order}. Read the sharps sentence from the end and you have the flats. Tap Next to add them one at a time.
music_cards_circle_order_next: {note} is next. The signature now has {count}.
music_cards_circle_order_ready_text: Next, name the sharps or flats of a key, in order: {sharps} for sharps, {flats} for flats. Go as fast as you can stay right.
music_cards_circle_order_sharps_text: Sharps always join a key signature in the same order: {order}. Remember it as Father Charles Goes Down And Ends Battle. Tap Next to add them one at a time.
music_cards_circle_order_title: The order of sharps and flats
music_cards_circle_relative_share_none: {major} major and {minor} minor share no sharps or flats.
music_cards_circle_relative_text: Every major key shares its signature with a minor key 3 half steps below its tonic. Count down 3 half steps from the major tonic.
music_cards_circle_secondary_any_text: A secondary dominant is a dominant seventh a fifth above the chord it leads to. It's written V of, or V/ followed by the target.
music_cards_circle_secondary_find_step: {name}: the target is {target}, a fifth above is {root}, so {dom}.
music_cards_circle_secondary_find_text: Name the target chord and go up a fifth. Make that a major chord with a flat seventh, even when the target is minor: E7 before Am, not Em7.
music_cards_circle_secondary_four_text: Tap each to hear the dominant resolve to its target.
music_cards_circle_secondary_four_title: Four in the key of C
music_cards_circle_secondary_v_of_c: G7 is the V of C, a fifth above C.
music_cards_circle_secondary_v_of_v: {dom} is V/V: a fifth above G, leading to G.
music_cards_circle_signature_bass_text: In bass clef the same signature sits on different lines. The order of the sharps and flats stays the same.
music_cards_circle_signature_ready_text: You see a signature and name the key. Count first, then apply the rule for sharps or flats. Speed comes with practice.
music_cards_circle_signature_rule_sharp: {accidentals}, the last is {last}. A half step up gives {key}.
music_cards_circle_signature_rule_text: With sharps, the key is a half step above the last sharp. With flats, it's the second-to-last flat, and F has 1 flat.
music_cards_circle_signature_staff_text: A key signature sits at the start of every line, after the clef. Count the sharps or flats and you know the key. Tap Next to see some.
music_cards_circle_signature_staff_title: Sharps and flats on the staff
music_cards_circle_wheel_cw_text: Going clockwise from C the keys are {keys}. Each is a fifth above the last. Tap Next to walk round.
music_cards_circle_wheel_flat_text: On the other side the keys, read clockwise towards C, are {keys}. Counter-clockwise from C they run F, Bb, Eb, Ab, Db.
music_cards_circle_wheel_meet_text: At the bottom the sharp and flat names meet: B or Cb, F# or Gb, Db or C#. The wheel shows B, F# and Db.
music_cards_connected_check_text: Check hides the notes, so know the order of the boxes and which way each one runs.
music_cards_connected_run_text: The connected run joins the five boxes into one line up the neck. It plays box 1 from the low string to the high, then box 2 from the high string back to the low. It carries on that way through box 5.
music_cards_connected_title: The boxes joined up the neck
music_cards_cs_minor_inside: It's all in C natural minor.
music_cards_cs_minor_outside_text: The altered V brings notes the key doesn't have, such as the B that leads up to C. The ii and the i stay close to the key. In Check the keys stay dark, so know each scale's notes.
music_cards_cs_minor_scale_text: Over each chord of a minor ii-V-i you play its go-to scale. In C minor, {s1} takes {l1}, {s2} takes {l2} and {s3} takes {l3}. Tap Next for the notes of each.
music_cards_dorian_all_text: The scale starts from a different note for each chord. Tap Next for each chord and whether its scale stays inside the key.
music_cards_dorian_scale_text: Over each chord of a ii-V-I you play its go-to scale. In C, {symbol} takes {scale}: {notes}. Those are the notes of C major, started on D, so nothing clashes with the key.
music_cards_ear_bass_intro_text: Chords play from I with their bass, and you write down the bass note of each as a scale degree. The bass is the chord's root, and at a higher level it can be another chord tone. Here the bass walks 1, 4, 5 under I, IV and V in C.
music_cards_ear_bass_intro_title: The lowest note of each chord
music_cards_ear_bass_root: Here the bass plays degree {degree}, the root of the {chord} chord: {above}.
music_cards_ear_bass_third: Here the {token} chord has its 3rd in the bass: degree {degree}, {above}.
music_cards_ear_cadence_line_authentic: It lands on I, home, so it sounds finished.
music_cards_ear_cadence_line_deceptive: V leads you to expect I, but it goes to vi instead.
music_cards_ear_cadence_line_half: It ends on V, so it sounds unfinished, like a pause.
music_cards_ear_cadence_line_plagal: It also lands on I, but it comes from IV instead of V.
music_cards_ear_cadences_intro_text: A cadence is two chords that end a phrase, like punctuation. The quiz plays two chords and you name the cadence by where they go. Here V goes to I, the cadence that sounds most finished.
music_cards_ear_cadences_intro_title: Two chords that close a phrase
music_cards_ear_cadences_item: {progression}. {line} Here it is in C, and the quiz moves it to other keys.
music_cards_ear_chord_item: {label} in {key} is {symbol}: a {word}. {root}. Here the key is set first with {call}.
music_cards_ear_colour_blues: the flat 5th, 6 half steps up, between the 4th and the 5th
music_cards_ear_colour_dorian: the minor 3rd with a major 6th, 9 half steps up
music_cards_ear_colour_harmonic_minor: the jump from the 6th, 8 half steps up, to the 7th, 11 half steps up
music_cards_ear_colour_locrian: the minor 2nd and the flat 5th, 1 and 6 half steps up
music_cards_ear_colour_major: the major 3rd, 4 half steps above the tonic
music_cards_ear_colour_major_pentatonic: five notes, with no 4th and no 7th
music_cards_ear_colour_melodic_minor: the minor 3rd with a major 6th and 7th, 9 and 11 half steps up
music_cards_ear_colour_minor_pentatonic: five notes, with no 2nd and no 6th
music_cards_ear_colour_mixolydian: the major 3rd with a minor 7th, 10 half steps up
music_cards_ear_colour_natural_minor: the minor 3rd, 3 half steps above the tonic
music_cards_ear_compare_intro_text: Two intervals play one after the other, and you say which one is bigger. Compare the distance between the notes in each, not how high they sound. Later the second interval can start on a different note.
music_cards_ear_degree_first_note: The tonic plays first, then this note.
music_cards_ear_degree_first_same: The tonic plays first, then the same note again.
music_cards_ear_degree_next_note: The tonic plays next, then this note.
music_cards_ear_degree_next_same: The tonic plays next, then the same note again.
music_cards_ear_degrees_intro_text: In a key, each note has a degree: 1 is the tonic, home, and the rest count up the scale. The quiz plays the tonic, then one more note, and you name its degree. Here are the degrees of C major.
music_cards_ear_feel_intro_text: A groove's feel is how it divides each beat. The quiz plays a groove and you name its feel from where the notes between the beats fall. Below, each beat split straight in two.
music_cards_ear_fine_intro_text: A cent is a hundredth of a half step. The quiz plays a note, then the same note a few cents higher or lower, or sometimes in tune, and you say which. The widest step is {cents} cents, and the steps run down to {smallest}.
music_cards_ear_functions_intro_text: The key is set with I, IV, V, I, then one chord plays and you name its numeral. The numeral is the chord's place in the key: I is built on the tonic, V on the 5th degree. The keys below show the chord built on each note of C major.
music_cards_ear_functions_intro_title: Each chord has a place in the key
music_cards_ear_intervals_any: The second note is {steps} above the first. The quiz can also play it coming down or together, with the same {steps}.
music_cards_ear_intervals_ascending: The second note is {steps} above the first, as the quiz plays it.
music_cards_ear_intervals_descending: The second note is {steps} below the first, as the quiz plays it.
music_cards_ear_intervals_harmonic: The two notes sound together, {steps} apart, as the quiz plays them.
music_cards_ear_intervals_intro_down: An interval is the distance between two notes, counted in half steps: one key to the very next, black keys included. {from} down to {to} is 4. Tap Next to count some, then the quiz plays two notes and you name the distance.
music_cards_ear_intervals_intro_up: An interval is the distance between two notes, counted in half steps: one key to the very next, black keys included. {from} up to {to} is 4. Tap Next to count some, then the quiz plays two notes and you name the distance.
music_cards_ear_intervals_unison: The same note twice, 0 half steps apart. Nothing moves between the two.
music_cards_ear_inversions_intro_text: An inversion is which note of the chord sits lowest. The quiz plays one chord, and you name the inversion by the note in the bass. Here C major has its 3rd, E, at the bottom: first inversion.
music_cards_ear_inversions_item: The {tone} of the chord is the lowest note, with the same note again an octave higher. Here, in {chord}, that's {note}.
music_cards_ear_key_changes_moves_text: The old key is set with I, IV, V, I, then a few chords take the music to a new key. You answer where it went, then name the chords as numerals in the new key. The last chord is the new tonic: here C moves up a whole step to D.
music_cards_ear_key_changes_ways_text: A ii-V, a V7 or a backdoor leads into a major key, here a whole step up. To a minor key the quiz uses {paths}.
music_cards_ear_key_set_first: The key is set first with {call}.
music_cards_ear_loops_intro_text: The key is set, then a loop of chords plays as a groove, and you name every chord as a numeral. A flat sign, as in bVII, means the chord's root is a half step lower than that degree in the major scale. The keys below show each numeral's root in C major.
music_cards_ear_melody_intro_text: The key is set first, then the tonic plays and a short phrase follows. You answer with its degrees in order, by playing or singing them back. This one is {answer}.
music_cards_ear_progressions_intro_text: A progression of three or four chords plays, always starting on I, and you write down the rest as numerals. Hearing where each chord sits in the key tells you which numeral it is. The keys below show each numeral's root in C major.
music_cards_ear_qualities_aug_text: Augmented is major with the 5th a half step higher: C, E, G#. It sounds stretched, as if it wants to move.
music_cards_ear_qualities_dim_text: Diminished is minor with the 5th a half step lower: C, Eb, Gb. It sounds tight and unsettled.
music_cards_ear_qualities_item: It stacks the {parts}. Listen for the {words}: {numbers} half steps above the root{no7}.
music_cards_ear_qualities_mm_text: A chord's quality comes from the notes stacked above its root: the 3rd and the 5th. The quiz plays one chord with all its notes at once, and you name the quality. Tap each to hear it: only the 3rd moves, 4 half steps above the root in major, 3 in minor.
music_cards_ear_root_above: Its root is {steps} above the tonic
music_cards_ear_scales_intro_text: The quiz holds the tonic low and plays a scale from it, and you name the scale. Each scale is a set of steps from the tonic, and one or two notes give it its colour. Here is C major, counted up from its tonic.
music_cards_ear_scales_item: Listen for {colour}. A low tonic holds under the scale, which here goes up.
music_cards_ear_wrong_intro_text: A melody is written as degrees, here {written}. It plays after its tonic with one note changed, here note {at}, and you say which place. Later it can also play exactly as written.
music_cards_fb_differing: from the {lo} to the {hi} it is {value}
music_cards_fb_fifth_text: A 5th is 7 half steps: the next string up{sep} {rel}{except}. Tap Next to see each pair of strings.
music_cards_fb_fourth_text: A 4th is 5 half steps. Strings are usually tuned {common} frets apart, so a 4th is the next string up{sep} {rel}{except}.
music_cards_fb_half_text: An interval is the distance between two notes, counted in half steps. One fret is one half step. A minor 3rd is 3, a major 3rd is 4, a 4th is 5, a 5th is 7 and an octave is 12.
music_cards_fb_high_g: The {names} string is tuned high, above the string next to it, so it sits apart from the rest.

match.countPlural=one: The irregular pair has a gap of {list} instead of {common}. A shape that crosses a smaller gap moves higher and a larger gap lower, by the difference. Tap Next to see the 5th across it.
match.countPlural=other: The irregular pairs have gaps of {list} instead of {common}. A shape that crosses a smaller gap moves higher and a larger gap lower, by the difference. Tap Next to see the 5th across each.

music_cards_fb_markers_guitar: The figure shows the dots at frets 3 and 5. Higher up there are dots at 7 and 9, and two at 12. Fret 12 is the open string's note an octave higher.
music_cards_fb_markers_ukulele: Ukuleles usually have dots at frets 5, 7, 10 and 12, with two at 12. They help you find your place. Fret 12 is the open string's note an octave higher.
music_cards_fb_match_step: Fret {fret} on the {lo} is the open {hi}.
music_cards_fb_naturals_text: The natural notes are A B C D E F G, then A again. There's a sharp between most of them, but not between B and C or between E and F. The {name} string below shows the naturals in its first five frets.
music_cards_fb_next_text: Fret {fret} on a string is the open note of the next string up in pitch.
music_cards_fb_next_text_reentrant: Fret {fret} on a string is the open note of the next string up, counting from the {from} and skipping the high {names} string.
music_cards_fb_oc_follows: When both gaps are {common} frets, the octave two strings up{notHigh} is {rel}.
music_cards_fb_oc_none: No two strings two apart here{notHigh} have both gaps of {common} frets.
music_cards_fb_octave_shapes_text: An octave is 12 half steps, which is 12 frets on one string.
music_cards_fb_open_text: The open strings are the notes you hear with no finger down. From string {count} to string 1 they are {notes}.
music_cards_fb_tap_next_pair: Tap Next to see each pair.
music_cards_fb_thirds_text: A major 3rd is 4 half steps: the next string up{sep} {rel}{except}. A minor 3rd is 3 half steps, always one fret lower than the major 3rd.
music_cards_formula_check_text: Check hides the notes, so the formula is your map. In any major scale the half steps fall between {pairs}. In C that's {names}.
music_cards_formula_gap_h_fret: a half step, the next fret on one string
music_cards_formula_gap_w_fret: a whole step, 2 frets on one string
music_cards_formula_steps_text: Every major scale follows one pattern of whole steps (W) and half steps (H): {formula}. Tap Next to build C major one step at a time.
music_cards_gloss_7alt: Alt is a dominant with altered tones in place of the 5th: {b9}, {s9}, {s11} and {b13}.
music_cards_gloss_m7b5: Minor with a flat 5th and a flat 7th, also called half-diminished.
music_cards_gloss_major: A root alone means a major triad.
music_cards_gospel_line_text: In C the bass plays {bass}. Follow it first, then fill in the chord above it. In Check the keys stay dark.
music_cards_gospel_moving_text: {about} The note after a slash is the bass, and with no slash the bass is the root. In C, tap Next for each chord.
music_cards_gospel_step: {symbol}: the bass is {bass} and the other notes are in {inversion}.
music_cards_guide_falls_text: In a ii-V-I the 7th of each chord falls a half step to the 3rd of the next: {a} to {b}, then {c} to {d} in C. The drill keeps every pair between F3 and C5, so in a low key a falling note may jump up an octave. In Check the keys stay dark, so find each pair from the chord before.
music_cards_guide_pair_text: A chord's 3rd and 7th say what kind of chord it is. The drill asks for those two notes of each chord in turn, through as many keys as the Keys setting says. Each time it asks for the pair nearest the one before.
music_cards_inversions_c_text: Tap Next for each chord and what carries over.
music_cards_inversions_c_title: I IV V I in C
music_cards_inversions_check_text: Check hides the keys, so work forward from the chord before. Ask which note stays, then where the others go.
music_cards_inversions_first_step: {symbol}: {inversion}, {notes}, over its root in the left hand.
music_cards_inversions_move_text: I IV V I in one key: a triad in the right hand over its root in the left. Aim to move the notes as little as you can from the chord before, keeping the notes the two chords share. In some keys the range of the keyboard forces a bigger move.
music_cards_inversions_move_text_arp: I IV V I in one key: a triad played one note at a time, above its root. Aim to move the notes as little as you can from the chord before, keeping the notes the two chords share. In some keys the range the drill uses forces a bigger move.
music_cards_inversions_move_title: Move as little as you can
music_cards_minor_natural_text: Natural minor follows {form}. The other two minor scales change its top notes. Harmonic minor raises the 7th by a half step, which leaves a step and a half under it.
music_cards_minor_three_text: Tap each form to hear it. Harmonic minor is {harmonic}, with {harmonicNotes} in A. Melodic minor, as the drill plays it, raises the 6th and 7th both ways: {melodic}, with {melodicNotes} in A.
music_cards_minor_v_altered_text: {symbol} uses the voicing "{voicing}". Its altered tones are the {tones}. {hint}
music_cards_minor_v_kinds_text: The minor ii-V-i is {chords} in C minor. The ii is half-diminished (m7b5: flat 3rd, flat 5th, flat 7th). The V is altered, and the i is a rootless minor 7th.
music_cards_minor_v_kinds_text_top: The minor ii-V-i is {chords} in C minor. The ii is half-diminished (m7b5: flat 3rd, flat 5th, flat 7th), voiced with the root on top. The V is altered, and the i is a rootless minor 7th.
music_cards_patterns_minor_text: The minor ii-V-i works the same way. On an altered chord the 5th is its flat 13th, and the 2nd or 9th is the flat 9th. In Check the keys stay dark, so know each pattern's notes.
music_cards_patterns_two_text: On each chord you play a four-note pattern up and back. 1-2-3-5 starts on the root, and 3-5-7-9 on the 3rd: tap each to see it on {symbol}. The 3rd, 5th and 7th are the chord's own, and the 2nd or 9th comes from its go-to scale.
music_cards_rootless_251_text: Tap Next for each chord. The drill can start on position B instead, which swaps A and B.
music_cards_rootless_leave_text: A rootless voicing leaves the root to the bass: the left hand plays the root, the right hand four chord notes above it. Tap Position A (the 3rd lowest) or Position B (the 7th lowest) to see and hear each on {symbol}.
music_cards_rootless_leave_text_arp: A rootless voicing leaves the root to the bass: you play the root, then four chord notes above it, one at a time. Tap Position A (the 3rd lowest) or Position B (the 7th lowest) to see and hear each on {symbol}.
music_cards_rootless_move_text: Between one chord and the next in the same key, each of the four upper notes moves a whole step at most, counting note names and ignoring which octave the keys show. Some don't move at all. In Check the keys stay dark, so work out each chord's notes from its position.
music_cards_rootless_step: {symbol}: position {pos}, {degrees} ({notes}) in the right hand over {root} in the left.
music_cards_symbols_root_text: A chord symbol starts with the root note. What follows says which chord it is. Tap Next to build each kind on C.
music_cards_symbols_slash_text: A note after a slash is the lowest note. C/E is a C chord with E in the bass, and Am/G is A minor with G in the bass. You choose how to place the notes.
music_cards_thumb_left_text: Going up, the left hand's 3rd or 4th finger crosses over its thumb. Going down, its thumb passes under. The fingers are the same each time round, so learn where the crossing falls in each key.
music_cards_thumb_left_title: The left hand does the reverse
music_cards_thumb_step_1: In C major the right hand plays {fingers}.
music_cards_thumb_step_2: The thumb passes under finger {finger} to play {note}.
music_cards_thumb_under_text: A scale is longer than five fingers reach, so the hand passes the thumb under. Going up with the right hand, the thumb passes under the 3rd or 4th finger. Going down, that finger crosses over the thumb.
music_cards_tier1_groove_all_text: Here is one bar of the simplest groove, counted 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 &, where & is the half beat. Tap Next to add the drums one at a time.
music_cards_tier1_groove_grid_text: In the drill, each drum is a row and each column is a count, and the picture shows the example filled in. Mark the squares where you heard a hit, then check. The levels go {levels}.
music_cards_tier1_groove_hat_text: The hi-hat keeps time with a steady run of hits. The first two levels play every eighth note, and the sixteenths and trap levels sometimes play every sixteenth.
music_cards_tier1_groove_kick_text: The kick is the low drum, and it lands on beat 1 of every bar in every groove here. The other kick hits move around from groove to groove. Tap Hear it for a kick on beats 1 and 3.
music_cards_tier1_groove_snare_text: The snare is the sharp crack on beats 2 and 4. The sixteenths level can add extra snare hits around it, and in trap the main snare moves to beat 3.
music_cards_tier1_home_cadence_text: Chords can lead away from home and back. Tap Next to hear one chord at a time.
music_cards_tier1_home_checked_text: The drill works out the key from the whole recording, so home belongs to the song and not to the stretch you looped. A minor key's home is its first note, and the relative key's tonic counts too, such as C and A. A song that changes key, or sits long away from home, can fool it.
music_cards_tier1_home_one_text: In most music one note feels like the place the music rests. That note is the tonic, or home, and the key is named for it: in {note} major home is {note}.
music_cards_tier1_home_recording_text: Listen for the note the music settles on, the one where it could stop. Play it on your instrument, sing it, or pick it from the notes below. The octave doesn't matter.
music_cards_tier1_home_resolve_text: A major scale climbs 1 to 7, then reaches 1 again. Tap Unresolved to stop on 7, then Resolved to step up home.
music_cards_tier1_home_step_3: It sounds unfinished and wants to go home.
music_cards_tier1_home_step_4: It sounds finished, because you're back home.
music_cards_tier1_idea_close: A 4-way close voicing puts a melody note on top with the next three chord tones close below it, all within an octave. The drill goes through a ii-V-I with each chord tone on top in turn. A major chord with its root on top takes the 6th instead of the 7th.
music_cards_tier1_idea_drop2: Drop-2 starts from the 4-way close voicing and drops its second voice from the top down an octave. That note goes in the left hand and the other three stay in the right. The chord spreads wider than the close voicing, with the same four notes.
music_cards_tier1_idea_evans: Bill Evans's spreads on a ii-V-I use three notes in the left hand and two in the right. The left hand plays the 3rd, 7th and 9th, and on the V the 7th, 3rd and 13th. The top right-hand note is the melody, with one voice under it.
music_cards_tier1_idea_garland: Red Garland's block chords on a 12-bar blues: the left hand plays the 3rd, 7th and 9th of the chord. The right hand plays the melody in octaves, with a note a 5th above the lower one between them. The drill gives one chord a bar.
music_cards_tier1_idea_locked: In George Shearing's locked hands the melody note is doubled an octave below in the left hand, with a 4-way close chord under it in the right. A melody note that belongs to the major 6th chord (root, 3rd, 5th or 6th) gets that chord. Any other melody note gets the diminished seventh chord.
music_cards_tier1_idea_monk: Thelonious Monk's shells on a 12-bar blues keep the root in the left hand. On the I the right hand plays the 3rd, b7 and root. On the IV and V it plays the 3rd and b7, with the root and b9 together on top, a half step apart.
music_cards_tier1_idea_quartal: A quartal stack is three notes a 4th apart, all in the left hand. The drill moves it up the dorian mode for two octaves. To stay in the mode, one of its 4ths is sometimes an augmented 4th.
music_cards_tier1_idea_quartal_tune: Every chord in a tune's changes gets a left-hand stack of two 4ths taken from the chord's scale, with one of the chord's guide tones inside it: the 3rd or 7th, the 4th on a sus chord, or the 6th on a sixth or diminished chord. A chord on a diminished scale, such as a b9 dominant or a diminished 7th, has no such stack, so it gets a tritone under a 4th. The picture shows the first chord.
music_cards_tier1_idea_sevenths: A seventh chord stacks the root, 3rd, 5th and 7th, all from the notes of the key. The chord on each degree gets its quality from the key: maj7 on the I and IV, m7 on the ii, iii and vi, 7 on the V and m7b5 on the vii. The drill plays them in root position, up the key and back.
music_cards_tier1_idea_slash_tune: Every chord in a tune's changes becomes a triad over its root, chosen by the chord type. A minor 7th, 7sus or dominant takes the major triad a whole step below the root. A major 7th takes the triad on its 5th, and a half-diminished chord the minor triad on its b3.
music_cards_tier1_idea_so_what: The So What chord is a stack of 4ths with a 3rd on top, all from the dorian mode. The two lowest notes go in the left hand and the other three in the right. To stay in the mode, a 4th can grow to an augmented 4th and the top 3rd can shrink to a minor 3rd.
music_cards_tier1_idea_sus: A 7sus chord voiced as a slash chord: the root and 5th in the left hand, and the major triad a whole step below the root in the right. For C7sus that triad is Bb major, written Bb/C. The right hand can use any inversion of the triad.
music_cards_tier1_idea_two_hand: A rootless voicing leaves the root to the bass. In a ii-V-I the left hand plays the 3rd and 7th (the 7th and 3rd on the V), and the right hand adds the 9th, 5th and 13th.
music_cards_tier1_idea_upper: Each dominant in a tune gets a 1-3-7 shell in the left hand and a triad on top that adds colour tones. A b9 mark takes the VI triad (b9 13). Otherwise a dominant that resolves to a minor chord, or is marked alt, #9 or b13, takes the bVI triad (#9 b13), and any other takes the II triad (9 #11 13).
music_cards_tier1_pads_band_text: In this drill the band plays a loop and you play any pads and any rhythm over it. It's scored on time, meaning how close your hits sit to the sixteenth grid, and on keeping every bar going. A bar counts as kept going when it has at least two hits.
music_cards_tier1_pads_fill_text: The grid shows a groove bar, then a fill bar with the same hi-hat and the snare playing eighths on 3 and 4. Hear it adds the crash and kick on the next bar's one. In the drill, with A fill every 4 or 8 bars set, the fill bar needs more hits than your usual bar and a hit on the next bar's one.
music_cards_tier1_pads_space_text: You don't have to fill every beat. This bar is only the kick and snare, with no hi-hat, and it still counts as kept going. Only a bar with no hits, or one hit, loses that part of the score.
music_cards_tier1_pads_vary_text: Keep a groove going and change a little each time round. Tap Plain to hear one bar twice, or Varied to hear it then the same bar with one more kick on the & of 4. The grid shows the plain bar until you tap one.
music_cards_tier1_role_3: {name} is the 3rd, which makes the chord major.
music_cards_tier1_role_R: {name} is the root, the note the chord is named for.
music_cards_tier1_role_b3: {name} is the 3rd, which makes the chord minor.
music_cards_tier1_role_other: {name} is a tone of the chord.
music_cards_tier1_stack_add_left: Add {note}, {interval} above {below}, in the left hand.
music_cards_tier1_stack_add_right: Add {note}, {interval} above {below}, in the right hand.
music_cards_tier1_stack_start_left: Start on {note}, the lowest note, in the left hand.
music_cards_tier1_stack_start_right: Start on {note}, the lowest note, in the right hand.
music_cards_tier1_stacked_text: Here is the first one the drill gives, {symbol}. Tap Next to add its notes from the bottom up.
music_cards_tier1_stacked_text_monk: Here is the first chord with a cluster, {symbol}. Tap Next to add its notes from the bottom up.
music_cards_tier1_tones_chord_text: Your answer should finish on a tone of the chord that's playing. {chord} is made of {names}, lit on the keys.
music_cards_tier1_tones_each_text: Tap Next to light the tones from the bottom up.
music_cards_tier1_tones_land_text: End your phrase on one of these tones and it sounds settled. Notes outside the chord are fine on the way there. The chord changes as the groove goes round, and the tones change with it.
music_cards_tier1_vibrato_bite_text: Hold a note and pulse your bite by wiggling your jaw lightly on the mouthpiece, with no hard squeeze. The Aerophone sends the bite as pitch bend, and the drill reads those values. If it says no bite arrived, set the bite to send pitch bend (E-Wind bite mode gives vibrato).
music_cards_tier1_vibrato_checks_text: The drill listens for {seconds} seconds from your first note. You pass with the rate within {tolerance} percent of the target and an evenness of at least {evenness} percent. It shows how deep your pulses are but doesn't score that: aim for a small, even wobble around the note, not a slide between notes.
music_cards_tier1_vibrato_hear_text: Each tap above alternates a note with the note a semitone below, one pair per pulse. The app can't bend a pitch, and real vibrato is much narrower than a semitone. So this shows the rate only, not the width.
music_cards_tier1_vibrato_pulses_text: The drill sets a tempo and a number of pulses a beat, so {slowPulses} a beat at {slowBpm} is {slowRate} pulses a second. The top setting, {topPulses} a beat at {topBpm}, is {topRate} a second, the going rate from Larry Teal. Tap each rate to hear it.
music_cards_tip_changes_guide_text: Some pairs of chords let a finger stay on its string or slide along it. Use that finger to guide the rest. Other pairs have none, so there you move every finger together.
music_cards_tip_changes_shape_text: Lift all your fingers together and put them down together, rather than one at a time. Picture the next shape before the change. Go slowly enough that every change is clean, then speed up, landing on the beat when a clock runs.
music_cards_tip_chords_listen_text: Sound the strings one at a time and listen: each should ring clearly, not buzz or fade. If one is dead, adjust the finger that should be pressing it, then play the shape again.
music_cards_tip_chords_shape_text: Press with the tips of your fingers, close behind the fret. Keep the fingers arched so none of them touches the string next to its own.
music_cards_tip_spider_even_text: Press just hard enough for a clear note, and lift a finger only as far as it needs. Aim for each note the same length and loudness, evenly on the click. Start at a tempo where it feels easy, then raise it.
music_cards_tip_spider_finger_text: Each finger has its own fret: the index the first, the middle the second, the ring the third and the little finger the fourth. The pattern says which finger plays next. Keep the hand where it is and move only the fingers.
music_cards_tip_strum_fret_text: Put every finger down before you strum, so all the strings are ready. Strum once, in one smooth downward motion across the strings the shape uses. Let it ring until the app has named it.
music_cards_tip_strum_missing_text: A dead or buzzing string usually has a finger resting on it, or pressing away from the fret. Press with the tip of the finger, close behind the fret. The app checks each chord tone, so a muted string can show up as a missing one.
music_cards_tip_two_hand_count_text: Both hands follow the same click, so count the beats out loud. Where both hands play on the same beat, aim to land them together.
music_cards_tip_two_hand_one_text: The Practise setting can ask for Left only or Right only. Learn each part that way first, then play Both hands.
music_cards_triads_check_text: Check hides the notes. Know the three inversions and where each sits, and play each from its lowest string up.
music_cards_triads_three_text_major: You can play a major triad in three inversions, each higher up the neck than the one before. The drill plays them on strings {first} to {last}. Tap Next for {root} major{tuning} at its lowest root fret.
music_cards_triads_three_text_minor: You can play a minor triad in three inversions, each higher up the neck than the one before. The drill plays them on strings {first} to {last}. Tap Next for {root} minor{tuning} at its lowest root fret.
music_cards_uke_one_text: A position of the minor pentatonic is one hand position{notes}. Here is position 1{tuning}, as the drill places it at its lowest root fret. The drill plays it from string {first} to string {last}.
music_cards_uke_one_title: A position is a hand position
music_cards_uke_up_text: The five positions climb the neck. Counted from the root fret on string 1{tuning}, the lowest fret of {list}. In Check the notes stay hidden, so know where each position starts.
